title: Have and Have Got: Possession and Activities
summary: Use have and have got to talk about what someone possesses or experiences. Use have, not have got, in expressions for meals, washing and everyday experiences.
learningObjectives: Express present possession using have or have got, including negatives and questions.
Use had, did not have and did ... have for past possession or conditions.
Describe meals and drinks with have or having instead of have got.
Use common activity expressions such as have a shower, have a rest and have a good time.

explanation.heading: Possession: have and have got
explanation.body: For possession in the present, both have and have got are common: I have a bike and I have got a bike mean the same thing. With have, questions and negatives usually use do/does. With have got, use have/has before the subject for questions and have not/has not for negatives.
explanation.example: Does Bea have a tablet, or has she got one?

explanation.heading: Health and the past tense
explanation.body: Use have or have got for conditions such as a cold, a headache or a sore throat. When talking about the past, use had; make past negatives and questions with did not have and did ... have. Do not use have got to express past possession.
explanation.example: I had a cold on Monday, but I feel much better now.

explanation.heading: Have with meals and drinks
explanation.body: For eating and drinking, use have breakfast, have lunch, have dinner, have a sandwich or have a drink. These describe an activity, not possession. Do not replace have with have got in this meaning. Use having when the activity is happening now.
explanation.example: We are having lunch in the garden today.

explanation.heading: Have for routines and experiences
explanation.body: Many fixed expressions use have: have a shower, have a bath, have a rest, have a party, have a holiday, have fun, have a good time, have a look and have a walk. You can also have an accident or have a baby. These expressions describe events or activities.
explanation.example: After the long journey, I had a rest.

explanation.heading: Having an activity versus having a possession
explanation.body: You can say I am having a shower because taking a shower is an activity. For ordinary possession, use I have or I have got rather than I am having. Context tells you whether have means own or do/experience.
explanation.example: We have a shower upstairs, and my brother is having a shower now.

left.label: Have
left.note: Use has with third-person singular subjects.

right.label: Have got
right.note: Has got expresses the same present possession.

comparisons.title: Owning something versus doing an activity

left.label: Have for possession
left.example: My flat has a large bathroom.
left.note: Has describes something the flat contains.

right.label: Have for an activity
right.example: I have a shower after work.
right.note: Have a shower describes washing, not owning a shower.

examples.sentence: Have you got any brothers or sisters?
examples.note: Have you got asks about present possession or family relationships.

examples.sentence: I did not have a phone when I was ten.
examples.note: Did not have expresses a negative in the past.

examples.sentence: My sister has got a headache today.
examples.note: Have got can express a current health condition.

examples.sentence: We had a lovely meal at the café yesterday.
They are having a party on Saturday.
examples.note: Having a party refers to a planned event.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We have got dinner at eight every evening.
commonMistakes.correct: We have dinner at eight every evening.
commonMistakes.why: For eating dinner, use have dinner, not have got dinner.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Did you had a car at university?
commonMistakes.correct: Did you have a car at university?
commonMistakes.why: Use the base form have after did.

commonMistakes.incorrect: My friends has got a new flat.
commonMistakes.correct: My friends have got a new flat.
commonMistakes.why: Friends is plural, so use have got.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She is having a red bicycle.
commonMistakes.why: For ordinary possession, use has, not is having.

studyTips: Ask whether have means possession or an activity: I have a camera, but I am having breakfast.
Memorise the past pattern: had a bike, did not have a bike, did you have a bike?
Practise short combinations such as have a rest, have a look, have fun and have a good time.

choices: Leo has a shower after school.
exercises.feedback: Has got a bicycle expresses possession; having a bicycle is not the normal possession form.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence about yesterday: Nina ___ a sore throat last night.
exercises.feedback: Had is the past form used for a past health condition.

exercises.prompt: Which question correctly asks about present possession?
choices: Do you got a new phone?
Have got you a new phone?
Have you got a new phone?
exercises.feedback: In a have got question, put have before the subject: Have you got ... ?

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means that she is eating lunch at this moment?
exercises.feedback: Is having lunch describes the meal in progress; has got can describe possession or acquisition.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the past form of have: We ___ a lovely time at the beach last weekend.
acceptedAnswers: had
exercises.feedback: Have a lovely time becomes had a lovely time in the past.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the present simple form of have: I ___ a shower every morning.
acceptedAnswers: have
exercises.feedback: Have a shower describes a routine activity.

exercises.prompt: Complete with one word: Ben does not ___ much free time on weekdays.
acceptedAnswers: have
exercises.feedback: After does not, use the base form have.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the -ing form of have: Look, the children are ___ a rest under the tree.
acceptedAnswers: having
exercises.feedback: Are having a rest describes an activity in progress.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence about a daily meal: We have got breakfast at seven every day.
acceptedAnswers: We have breakfast at seven every day.
exercises.feedback: Have breakfast means eat breakfast; have got does not express this activity.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Did you had enough money for the ticket?
acceptedAnswers: Did you have enough money for the ticket?
exercises.feedback: Use the base form have after did.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence about possession: She is having a new bike. It belongs to her.
acceptedAnswers: She has a new bike. It belongs to her.
She has got a new bike. It belongs to her.
She's got a new bike. It belongs to her.
exercises.feedback: Ordinary possession uses has or has got, not is having.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: My friends hasn't got a car.
acceptedAnswers: My friends haven't got a car.
My friends have not got a car.
exercises.feedback: A plural subject requires have, so the negative is have not got or haven’t got.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change this sentence to use have got: “Mina has two sisters.”
acceptedAnswers: Mina has got two sisters.
Mina's got two sisters.
speakingExercises.feedback: Has got expresses the same present relationship as has.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change this sentence into the past: “We have a good time at the fair.”
acceptedAnswers: We had a good time at the fair.
speakingExercises.feedback: Had is the past form of have.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say a complete present continuous sentence from these cues: Dad / have / a shower / right now.
acceptedAnswers: Dad is having a shower right now.
Dad's having a shower right now.
speakingExercises.feedback: Is having a shower describes an activity happening now.

speakingExercises.prompt: Leila has a sore throat today. Say one complete sentence beginning with Leila and using has got for her condition. Include today.
acceptedAnswers: Leila has got a sore throat today.
Leila's got a sore throat today.
speakingExercises.feedback: Has got can describe a present health condition; Leila's got is a natural contraction.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change 'Marco has a small car.' into a negative present-simple sentence. Use doesn't or does not, and keep a small car.
acceptedAnswers: Marco doesn't have a small car.
Marco does not have a small car.
speakingExercises.feedback: With does not or doesn't, use the base verb have, not has.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend asks whether you had a headache yesterday. The answer is no. Give a complete negative sentence beginning with I and ending with yesterday.
acceptedAnswers: I didn't have a headache yesterday.
I did not have a headache yesterday.
speakingExercises.feedback: A past negative uses did not have or didn't have, never did not had.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct this sentence so that it describes eating a meal right now, using are having: 'The twins have got lunch right now.' Keep the other words and say the full sentence.
acceptedAnswers: The twins are having lunch right now.
speakingExercises.feedback: Are having lunch describes the activity of eating. Have got does not express a meal in progress.

speakingExercises.prompt: You own a blue umbrella, and your sister is taking a rest right now. Say one sentence beginning with I. Use have got for the umbrella and is having for the rest, joining the clauses with and.
acceptedAnswers: I have got a blue umbrella and my sister is having a rest right now.
I've got a blue umbrella and my sister is having a rest right now.
I have got a blue umbrella and my sister's having a rest right now.
I've got a blue umbrella and my sister's having a rest right now.
speakingExercises.feedback: Have got expresses possession of the umbrella; is having a rest describes an activity in progress.

listeningExercises.audioText: My cousin has got two cats and a small dog.
listeningExercises.prompt: How many cats does the speaker’s cousin have?
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker says the cousin has got two cats.

listeningExercises.audioText: We had a wonderful time at the concert last night.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker say about the concert?
listeningExercises.feedback: Had a wonderful time expresses a positive experience.

listeningExercises.audioText: Oliver is having a shower before work.
listeningExercises.prompt: Complete the expression you hear: “Oliver is ___ a shower before work.” Type one word.
acceptedAnswers: having
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker says is having a shower to describe an activity in progress.

listeningExercises.audioText: It is nearly noon, and Emma is having a snack before her music lesson.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is Emma doing before her lesson?
listeningExercises.feedback: Having a snack means eating some food; here having describes an activity.

listeningExercises.audioText: When Daniel was eight, he did not have a bicycle, but now he has got one.
choices: He sold a bicycle he had as a child.
He still does not own a bicycle.
He owns a bicycle now, unlike when he was eight.
listeningExercises.feedback: He did not have a bicycle at eight, but has got one now. The first expression is past possession; the second is present possession.

listeningExercises.audioText: I have a camera, but I am having breakfast before I take any pictures.
choices: The speaker is eating a morning meal.
The speaker is buying a camera.
listeningExercises.feedback: Am having breakfast describes an activity now; have a camera describes possession.

listeningExercises.audioText: My grandparents have got a small house near the sea.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word present-possession expression heard immediately after 'grandparents'.
acceptedAnswers: have got
listeningExercises.feedback: Have got describes something the grandparents own in the present.

listeningExercises.audioText: We had a rest in the shade after working in the garden.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word expression meaning 'took a break' in the recording.
acceptedAnswers: had a rest
listeningExercises.feedback: Had a rest is the past form of the activity expression have a rest.
